notes: Short criminal appeal on meaning of 'accident' in aggravated vehicle taking; ratio and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Aggravated vehicle taking where death caused by deliberate driving
key_facts: The appellant pleaded guilty to aggravated vehicle taking after being convicted of murder for deliberately driving a stolen Ford Mondeo over Mr Glyn Ellis.
Count 3 alleged that Mr Ellis's death was caused by an accident within the meaning of section 12A of the Theft Act 1968.
The appellant argued that once the jury found intent to kill or do really serious harm on the murder count, conviction on count 3 was inconsistent and count 3 should have been left on the file.
He also sought to renew an application for leave to appeal against the murder conviction, alleging he was wrongly persuaded not to give evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave against conviction on count 3, with a renewed application for leave to appeal against the murder conviction.
enrichment.outcome: Both grounds dismissed; count 3 is not a true alternative to murder and an 'accident' under section 12A may include a deliberate act with adverse physical results.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 12A of the Theft Act 1968, 'accident' is not limited to unintended occurrences; it may include an untoward occurrence with adverse physical results even where a deliberate act forms part of the chain of events, and aggravated vehicle taking is concerned with consequences rather than whether count 3 is an alternative to murder.
legal_issues: Whether conviction for aggravated vehicle taking is inconsistent with a murder conviction on the same facts
Meaning of 'accident' in section 12A(2)(b) of the Theft Act 1968
Whether count 3 should have been left on the file under R v Cole
Whether the murder conviction was unsafe
linked_authorities: R v Morris (1972) 56 Cr App R 175
R v Cole (1965) 49 Cr App R 199

notes: Preliminary limitation issue after CMA CGM; charterer claims against owners held not limitable as consequential vessel damage.

enrichment.short_title: Limitation of owners' liability to time charterers after Darfur collision

statutes_considered.title: Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims 1976

key_facts: The m/v Darfur collided with the Happy Fellow on the River Seine in November 1995, causing vessel damage, salvage costs, and cargo-related claims.
Blue Nile, the Darfur owners, constituted a limitation fund in England while parallel French collision proceedings continued.
Baco-Liner, the time charterers, brought English claims for off-hire, substitute vessel costs, insurance, transhipment, and related losses after admitting Blue Nile's liability.
The preliminary issue was whether Baco-Liner's remaining claims were limitable under the 1976 Convention.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a preliminary issue in an admiralty limitation action on whether charterers' claims must be brought against the limitation fund.
enrichment.outcome: Heads of claim consequential upon damage to the Darfur are not limitable; owners cannot limit liability to charterers in respect of those items, following CMA CGM v Classica.
enrichment.ratio: Following CMA CGM S.A. v Classica Shipping Co Ltd, loss or damage to the vessel whose tonnage fixes the limit, and consequential loss arising from such damage, fall outside Article 2(1)(a) and (f) of the 1976 Convention; that analysis applies whether owners seek to limit against charterers or charterers against owners.
legal_issues: Whether time charterers' claims against owners are maritime claims subject to limitation
Scope of Article 2(1)(a), (c) and (f) of the 1976 Convention
Whether off-hire, substitute vessel, insurance, and related losses are limitable
Application of CMA CGM v Classica to owner-charterer limitation disputes
linked_authorities: CMA CGM S.A. v Classica Shipping Co Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 114
Blue Nile Shipping Co Ltd v Sloman Neptune [1998] 1 Lloyd's Rep 13
Blue Nile Shipping Co Ltd v Sloman Neptune [1997] 1 Lloyd's Rep 130

notes: Detailed CPR service ruling on last known place of business and CPR 7.6 extension; outcome is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Invalid service on architect in warehouse fire claim
key_facts: Multi-party claims exceeding £16.5 million arose from a 1997 fire at a fruit storage warehouse at Spade Lane, Sittingbourne.
Mr Kilgour, an architect defendant, moved his practice from Studio 531 to Rosewood House in April 1998 and renamed the firm MKA Chartered Architects.
Claimants issued the claim form on 1 August 2003 and posted it to the obsolete Studio 531 address on 26 November 2003, near the four-month service deadline.
Assignor knowledge from 1998 dealings with Mr Kilgour was imputed to assignee claimants, and no extension application was made promptly.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue on whether the claim form was validly served on the fourth defendant under CPR Part 6.5 and, alternatively, whether time for service should be extended.
enrichment.outcome: No valid service; claimants failed to take all reasonable steps to ascertain Mr Kilgour's last known place of business and did not act promptly on any extension application.
enrichment.ratio: 'Last known place of business' in CPR 6.5(6) means the last place of business known to the claimant after reasonable enquiries; where service fails for insufficient investigation and late issue near limitation, CPR 7.6(3) will not readily extend time, especially if the defendant did not waive irregularities.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'last known place of business' in CPR 6.5(6)
Whether assignor knowledge of a defendant's address is imputed to assignee claimants
When the court may extend time for service under CPR 7.6(2) and 7.6(3)
Effect of Hashtroodi v Hancock on late service applications
linked_authorities: Vinos v Marks & Spencer plc [2001] 3 All ER 784

notes: Long Chancery trial on easements, way of necessity, estoppel and overriding interests; conclusions are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Vehicular right of way over neighbour's yard after conveyancing mistake
key_facts: Forge Meadow at Osbaston could only be accessed by vehicle by crossing the Old Forge Yard owned by the defendants.
A 1988 conveyancing mistake left Mr Lovering without power to grant the Martins a formal vehicular easement over the yard he had transferred to himself and his wife.
The Martins built and used a house on Forge Meadow believing they had a vehicular right of way; the first defendant bought the Old Forge with notice of that use.
A separate purported right of way over the northern field failed for want of a deed, leaving an equitable interest only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of claims for declarations of vehicular and pedestrian rights of way, rectification-related title issues, and injunctive relief against obstruction.
enrichment.outcome: Claimants entitled to a vehicular right of way over the Old Forge Yard for Forge Meadow by implied reservation and proprietary estoppel, and to an equitable right for the northern field as an overriding interest; injunctive relief and title amendments ordered in principle.
enrichment.ratio: A 1988 transfer that left retained land landlocked impliedly reserved a vehicular way of necessity over the granted yard for contemplated residential development; the Martins acquired a binding equitable easement by proprietary estoppel against successors with notice, and openly exercised rights could qualify as overriding interests under Rule 258 despite registry mistakes.
legal_issues: Whether Forge Meadow has a legal vehicular easement over the Old Forge Yard
Implied reservation of a way of necessity after a defective 1988 transfer
Whether proprietary estoppel binds the first defendant as successor in title
Whether the northern field enjoys an overriding easement under Rule 258

ER Ives Investment Ltd v High [1967] 2 QB 379
Celsteel Ltd v Alton House Ltd [1985] 1 WLR 204

notes: Commercial fraud and jurisdiction decision; service out upheld but arbitration stay granted under section 9.

enrichment.short_title: Service out upheld but arbitration stay in Liechtenstein foundation fraud claim
key_facts: Ms King invested about £4.5 million through financial adviser Mr Tune into a Liechtenstein foundation and related offshore annuities and companies.
Most funds were directed into Isosafe Limited and unsecured loans via BV Post, despite Ms King's requirement for safe long-term investments.
Isosafe collapsed and money was diverted through Coolbox and entities managed by Bryan and Alexander Jeeves of the Jeeves Group.
Ms King sued Mr Tune for deceit and the Jeeves as joint tortfeasors after they executed investment instructions procured by his alleged fraud.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside permission to serve the Jeeves out of the jurisdiction and, alternatively, to stay proceedings under section 9 of the Arbitration Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to serve out upheld; proceedings against the Jeeves stayed because the tort claim arose from the Contract of Mandate containing an arbitration clause.
enrichment.ratio: The claimant had a good arguable title to sue and a properly pleaded joint tortfeasor claim against the Jeeves, but a deceit claim closely connected to alleged bad-faith execution of mandated dispositions 'arises from' the 1997 Contract of Mandate and must be stayed in favour of arbitration under section 9.
legal_issues: Whether Ms King could sue in her own name rather than through the foundation or Lemur
Whether the claim against the Jeeves disclosed a cause of action as joint tortfeasors
Whether knowing assistance suffices for secondary liability
Whether the tort claim must be stayed under section 9 of the Arbitration Act 1996
linked_authorities: Credit Lyonnais Bank Nederland NV v Export Credits Guarantee Department [1998] 1 Lloyd's Rep 19

notes: Collective enfranchisement resident landlord exception; statutory interpretation point resolved unanimously.

enrichment.short_title: Resident landlord exception and continuity of freehold ownership

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform (Housing and Urban Development) Act 1993

key_facts: Two long leaseholders of flats at 50 Woodsome Road sought collective enfranchisement of the three-flat house.
The freeholder relied on the resident landlord exception because her mother had occupied a flat for twelve months and the family had owned the house since before conversion.
Between March 1998 and September 1999 legal title was held by the defendant's mother while the defendant held a beneficial interest under a declaration of trust.
Conversion works were completed between 1987 and 1991, and the section 13 notice was served on 6 November 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court decision upholding the resident landlord exception to collective enfranchisement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the defendant failed the continuous ownership test in section 10(1)(b) and section 10(4).
enrichment.ratio: For the resident landlord exception, continuity must be assessed from the section 13 notice back to before conversion; where the freehold is held on trust at the relevant date section 10(4) replaces the freehold ownership test with continuous interest under the trust, and mixed or interrupted legal and beneficial interests do not satisfy the statutory language.
legal_issues: Whether the defendant had owned the freehold continuously since before conversion
Interaction of section 10(1)(b) and section 10(4) where title moved into and out of trust
Whether family trust arrangements should be treated as continuous ownership
Proper construction of the 2002 amendments to section 10

notes: Covenant construction appeal on 'a private dwellinghouse'; Court of Appeal allowed appeal with full reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Restrictive covenant 'a private dwellinghouse' not a numerical limit
key_facts: Telford Development Corporation sold large plots on the Donnerville Estate with identical restrictive covenants in 1988.
Mr Martin owns plot 1 and claimed the benefit of covenants restricting plots 2 and 3 to a single dwelling house each.
David Wilson Homes wished to build twelve houses on part of plot 2 and had built a show house on plot 3.
The disputed covenant prohibited use of buildings otherwise than as 'a private dwellinghouse either with or without garages and other necessary outbuildings'.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue decision on construction of a restrictive covenant in schedule 6(c) of the conveyance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the phrase restricts manner of use, not the number of dwelling houses permitted on the plot.
enrichment.ratio: Read in context with neighbouring covenant clauses referring to 'any buildings' and 'any part thereof', 'a private dwellinghouse' in a user covenant is a manner-of-use restriction and does not limit the plot to one dwelling; the indefinite article does not necessarily connote singularity.
legal_issues: Whether 'a private dwellinghouse' limits the number of dwellings on a plot
Construction of schedule 6(c) against surrounding covenant clauses
Relevance of the sale contract requirement to build one house within eighteen months
Effect of Dobbs v Linford and Crest Nicholson on similar wording
linked_authorities: Crest Nicholson Residential (South) Ltd v McAllister [2003] 1 All ER 46

enrichment.short_title: Criminal injuries exclusion for foster child living with assailants
key_facts: Claimant M, taken into care in 1972, was placed with foster parents Mr and Mrs H in 1973 and suffered repeated non-accidental injuries including a severe shaking injury in March 1974.
He first claimed compensation in 1990 under the 1969 Criminal Injuries Compensation Scheme and later pursued an appeal after awards were set aside on eligibility.
Paragraph 7 of the 1969 scheme excludes compensation where victim and offender were living together as members of the same family at the time.
Boarding-out regulations required foster parents to receive the child to live in their dwelling as a member of their family.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Criminal Injuries Compensation Appeal Panel decision on eligibility under paragraph 7 of the 1969 scheme, part heard pending a Convention compatibility argument.
enrichment.outcome: Eligibility challenge rejected on the paragraph 7 'same family' point; proceedings adjourned to await the Scottish Smillie Convention challenge.
enrichment.ratio: A child boarded out under the Children Act 1948 and Boarding-Out Regulations to live as a member of the foster parents' family was, on the ordinary meaning of paragraph 7, living together with the assailants as a member of the same family and therefore excluded from the 1969 scheme.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'living together as members of the same family' in paragraph 7 of the 1969 scheme
Whether a foster child boarded out under the 1955 Regulations falls within the exclusion
Distinction between household and family in the boarding-out framework
Whether paragraph 7 is compatible with the European Convention on Human Rights

notes: Winding-up restraint appeal on Bayoil principles; live dispute now costs-only but reasoning is full.

enrichment.short_title: Winding-up petition allowed despite post-dated cheque dispute
key_facts: Thompson Shaw Associates LLP split under a September 2003 retirement agreement, with Marchands buying part of the business and post-dated cheques payable to Mr Shaw.
Payment depended on Completion Accounts showing excess capital and current account balances for Mr Shaw and Mr Brook.
The Partnership stopped a £14,000 cheque in November 2003, asserting Mr Shaw owed over £200,000 and had failed to deliver proper Completion Accounts.
Marchands presented a winding-up petition; the judge refused to restrain advertisement, but the petition was later dismissed after payment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal to restrain advertisement of a partnership winding-up petition based on dishonoured post-dated cheques.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the petition should have been dismissed or stayed because the Partnership had a genuine and serious cross-claim overtopping the petition debt.
enrichment.ratio: Where a limited liability partnership disputes post-dated cheques on substantial grounds and has a genuine cross-claim exceeding the petition debt which it has been unable to litigate, the Companies Court should dismiss or stay a winding-up petition even though cheques are ordinarily payable on presentation; contractual completion-account machinery is not a special reason to permit winding up.
legal_issues: Whether the petition debt was disputed on substantial grounds
Whether the Partnership had a cross-claim overtopping the petition debt
Effect of clause 4 and clause 6 completion-account procedures on winding-up practice
Whether failure of consideration or misrepresentation provided a defence to the cheques
linked_authorities: Cornhill Insurance Plc v Improvement Services Ltd [1986] 1 WLR 1014
